target.title: Deep Lip Reading: a comparison of models and an online application
target.venue: Proc. Interspeech 2018, pp. 3514-3518 (arXiv:1806.06053v1, 15 Jun 2018, first public)
target.version: arXiv v1 (2018-06-15); Interspeech 2018 version checked: same key passages and the same 22 percentage values

read.pdf: Figs. 1–2 and Tables 1–5 read in text.txt; PDF not separately supplied

entries.text: The authors claim three complementary new lip-reading models, adapting machine-translation and ASR architectures to lip reading for the first time.
entries.condition: Novelty claim in the introduction; models are BLSTM-CTC, fully convolutional-CTC, and Transformer.
entries.quote:
we adapt architectures developed for other domains,
namely machine translation and ASR, and repurpose them for
lip reading for the ﬁrst time.

entries.text: The authors claim a new state of the art on LRS2 and an improvement exceeding 20% over the previous 70.4% WER result.
entries.condition: Authors compare Transformer at 50.0% WER with T2 decoding against a prior 70.4% WER result; exact interpretation of percent versus percentage points is not defined.
entries.quote:
The best performing
network is the Transformer, which achieves a WER of 50%
when decoded with a language model trained on T 2, an im-
provement of over 20% compared to the previous 70.4% state-
of-the-art [6].

entries.text: The authors claim the fully convolutional model can decode continuous speech online, with high performance and low latency.
entries.condition: Qualitative online claim; online CER/WER and measured end-to-end latency are not reported.
entries.quote: In this section we describe how the FC model can be used for online lip reading with low latency.

entries.text: The authors say they will publicly release the networks, but the paper gives no repository URL.
entries.condition: No linked repository or code URL appears in text.txt; no code-only conditions could be checked.

entries.text: The models take silent talking-face video and share a visual front-end that processes loosely cropped lip regions into one feature vector per frame.
entries.condition: Visual input only; the common spatio-temporal front-end precedes each sequence backend.

entries.text: The shared visual front-end uses a five-frame 3D convolution followed by a 2D ResNet and emits 512-dimensional features at the input temporal resolution.
entries.condition: Common front-end for BL, FC-10, FC-15, and TM; spatial dimensions are downsampled by 32 before spatial average pooling.

entries.text: Visual inputs are grayscale, scaled, and centrally cropped; augmentation includes horizontal flips, random frame removal, spatial shifts up to ±5 pixels, and temporal shifts up to ±2 frames.
entries.condition: Applied while pretraining the visual front-end on LRW and MV-LRS(w). Exact pixel scaling/normalization parameters are not stated.

entries.text: The front-end is pretrained on word-level LRW and MV-LRS(w) data to classify each video with its word label.
entries.condition: Word-level classification pretraining precedes sequence-model training; MV-LRS(w) is derived from aligned sentence excerpts.
entries.quote: we pre-train the visual front-end on the word-level datasets

entries.text: Sequence models are trained on precomputed visual features, first using MV-LRS and LRS2 pre-train, then fine-tuned on LRS2 train with a word-count curriculum starting at two-word utterances.
entries.condition: Features are extracted with the pretrained visual front-end; curriculum adds longer utterances; LRS2 test set is used only for evaluation as described.
entries.quote: starts with utterances of 2 words then of 2 and 3 words then {2, 3, 4} etc.

entries.text: Variable-length utterances are zero-padded, and the maximum sequence length increases along with the maximum word count at each curriculum stage.
entries.condition: Sequence-model training curriculum.

entries.text: BL consists of three stacked bidirectional LSTM layers and is trained with CTC.
entries.condition: BL recurrent backend; CTC blank is added to the output alphabet.

entries.text: FC uses depth-wise separable temporal convolutions with shortcut connections, batch normalization, and ReLU, in 10-layer and 15-layer variants trained with CTC.
entries.condition: FC-10 and FC-15 sequence backends; both use the shared visual front-end.

entries.text: Transformer uses six encoder and six decoder layers, model size 512, eight attention heads, and dropout 0.1; it is trained with cross-entropy and teacher forcing.
entries.unit: encoder layers; decoder layers; model size; heads; dropout probability
entries.condition: Base Transformer; no explicit LM is used for the T1 result, while an external LM is integrated for T2.

entries.text: The character LM is a four-layer unidirectional recurrent network with 1,024 LSTM cells per layer.
entries.condition: Inference-time LM architecture shared across models; LM predicts one character at a time.
entries.quote: During inference we use a character-level language model, which is a recurrent network with 4 unidirectional layers of 1024 LSTM cells each.

entries.text: T2 uses 26M words of full subtitles from videos used to generate the LRS2 training set.
entries.condition: T2 contains more text than T1; this distinction affects explicit LM decoding and the Transformer T2 result.

entries.text: Evaluation reports CER and WER, defined as normalized edit distance between ground-truth and predicted sentences.
entries.condition: LRS2 test set; exact text normalization, tokenization, case, and punctuation handling are not specified.

entries.text: Models are implemented in TensorFlow and trained on one GeForce GTX 1080 Ti GPU with 11GB of memory.
entries.condition: Applies to the reported training runs.

entries.text: BL uses SGD with momentum 0.9 and learning rate 10⁻² reduced on plateaus to 10⁻⁴; FC and Transformer use Adam with initial rate 10⁻³ reduced on plateaus to 10⁻⁴.
entries.unit: momentum; BL initial LR; final LR; FC/TM initial LR
entries.condition: BL uses fixed momentum SGD; FC and TM use Adam default parameters; learning-rate reductions are triggered by plateauing error.

entries.text: Training dropout is 0.3 on Transformer inputs and BLSTM inputs/recurrent units, and 0.8 after every FC batch-normalization layer.
entries.condition: Architecture-specific dropout in sequence-model training; Transformer architecture section separately gives base-model dropout 0.1.

entries.text: Transformer T1 decoding uses beam width 5, α=0.0, β=0.6; T2 decoding uses width 15, α=0.1, β=0.7, selected by validation-set grid search.
entries.unit: beam width; α; β; beam width; α; β
entries.condition: T1 without external LM and T2 with external LM, respectively; hyperparameters selected on the validation set; no coverage penalty was tested.
entries.quote: for decoding without the external language model (T1) they were set to W = 5 ,α = 0.0,β = 0.6

entries.text: CTC beam decoding uses width 100, α=0.5, β=0.1, with length normalization |y|^β; the paper does not identify the data used to select these settings.
entries.condition: CTC models with external LM; selection/validation set for these best-result settings is not stated.
entries.quote: We obtain the best results withW = 100,α = 0.5,β = 0.1.

entries.text: Authors state FC-15's five extra layers reduce WER by 2% relative to FC-10, attributing the gain mostly to a wider receptive field.
entries.condition: Comparison of FC-10 and FC-15; error-rate protocol is LRS2 test; Table 1 T2 WERs are 57.1% and 55.0%, respectively.

entries.text: Authors claim depth-separable convolutions double FC training speed without reducing accuracy.
entries.condition: Claim concerns the fully convolutional architecture; no isolated ablation values are reported in the cited passage.
entries.quote: Using depth-separable convolutions doubles the network training speed

entries.text: Authors claim FC is smaller and trains faster than BL and Transformer while achieving 55% WER.
entries.condition: FC refers to the fully convolutional models; 55% corresponds to FC-15 T2 WER on LRS2 test, while Table 1 reports 55.0%.

entries.text: Authors report a 0.7–1.3% WER improvement for T2 versus T1 across the models.
entries.condition: Comparison of external language-model text corpora T1 and T2 across reported models; paper's percent wording does not clarify percentage points versus relative percent.
entries.quote: For all models we get an improvement of 0.7 - 1.3 % in WER when decoding with T2 compared to T1.

entries.text: The narrative gives FC-15 curriculum completion time as approximately 3.5 days, versus 13 days for Transformer; Table 1 gives 3.4 days for FC-15.
entries.condition: Full sequence-model curriculum; one GPU; visual-front-end pretraining excluded. Table/text discrepancy for FC-15 is recorded rather than reconciled.

entries.text: Authors say FC generalizes to longer sequences once training covers its full receptive field; accuracy gains diminish beyond 80 frames, and they report similar findings for BL.
entries.condition: Sequence length in training; not a test-set metric. TM generalized less well beyond training lengths.

entries.text: Authors report that Transformer generalized poorly to sequences longer than those seen in training and therefore extended the curriculum to the longest validation example.
entries.condition: Validation-set maximum sequence length determined the extended training curriculum; whether validation was also used for other model choices is described only for Transformer decoding hyperparameters.

entries.text: Authors suggest BL's weaker result may stem from CTC's local nature and monotonic alignment, which can limit the BLSTM's use of long-term dependencies for grammar.
entries.condition: Authors frame this as a suspicion, not a tested causal result; BL performs worse than FC-10 despite full context.
entries.quote: the output labels are not conditioned on each other and a monotonic alignment is enforced.

entries.text: Authors characterize online lip-reading work as a preliminary investigation.
entries.condition: Online FC decoding is presented separately from the offline Table 1 benchmark; the conclusion gives no online CER/WER or measured latency.

entries.text: The online FC setup reports lookahead of 22 and 32 future frames for its 11- and 16-layer configurations, respectively, including the front-end 3D convolutions.
entries.condition: Temporal convolution kernel K=5; computed lookahead r includes the front-end's 3D convolution contribution; configurations are described as 11- and 16-layer models.
entries.quote: In our setting withK = 5, r is equal to 22 and 32 frames for the 11 and 16 layer models respectively

entries.text: The online procedure processes new frames with a lag of r, updates a beam search incrementally, and can issue a current prediction at each decoding time step.
entries.condition: FC CTC model with language-model beam search; theoretical total complexity is O(TrW|A|). The paper does not report measured end-to-end latency.

entries.text: Table 5 lists 0.4 and 0.5 changes per frame for the illustrated beginning-of-utterance and middle-start online outputs.
entries.condition: Illustrative sequential online decoding examples only; not a benchmark or an aggregate accuracy measure.

entries.text: The online example notes that early frames lack sufficient context before predictions become correct.
entries.condition: Qualitative example in Table 5, not a scored online test result.

entries.condition: Appendix A.3 discusses Transformer beam-search scoring and validation-selected hyperparameters.

questions.q: Does the reported evidence support the paper's LRS2 state-of-the-art claim, and what decoding conditions qualify it?
questions.answer: The best reported result is Transformer WER 50.0% on the 1,243-utterance LRS2 test set with T2 external-LM decoding, versus the cited prior 70.4% WER. The paper states an improvement of over 20%, but does not define whether this means relative percent or percentage points; the prior row's decoding details are not separately specified.

questions.q: How strong is the empirical support for the online low-latency claim?
questions.answer: The paper gives an incremental FC/CTC beam-search algorithm, theoretical complexity, lookahead estimates of 22 and 32 future frames, and sample outputs. It calls the investigation preliminary and supplies no measured online latency or scored online CER/WER, so the low-latency claim is not quantified by an online benchmark.

questions.q: What evaluation and reproducibility qualifications should accompany the offline benchmark numbers?
questions.answer: The paper specifies the LRS2 test split size and the decode regimes, but reports no seeds or repetitions, speaker/session composition or overlap, chance baseline, or exact text-normalization rules. Transformer decoding parameters were selected on validation; the selection data for the reported CTC beam settings are not identified.
